item.title: New farming equipment for Tonga's organic farmers
item.description: Seventy-eight organic farmers across Tonga have received essential farming equipment to help strengthen agroecological and organic farming practices. The distribution coordinated by the Pacific Community ( SPC ), went to farmers on Tonga's two main island groups: Tongatapu and Vava'u.
item.content:encoded:
Seventy-eight organic farmers across Tonga have received essential farming equipment to help strengthen agroecological and organic farming practices.

The distribution coordinated by the Pacific Community ( SPC ), went to farmers on Tonga's two main island groups: Tongatapu and Vava'u.

The support is part of the Pacific Organic Learning Farms Network ( POLFN ) project's commitment to improving farmers' access to appropriate tools and technologies that enhance productivity, resilience, and sustainable agricultural practices.

Farmers received a range of equipment, including machetes, soil augers, drip irrigation systems, chainsaws, and weed eaters, to support their day-to-day farming activities.

Farmer and Women’s group leader, Melesila Weilert, Tongatapu, shared that the support comes at a crucial time for their community, where many residents have left to participate in seasonal work programmes in Australia and New Zealand.

“With a population of around 226 people in our village, many have joined the seasonal worker programmes overseas. Those of us who remain and are still able to do the physical work are mostly women,” she said.

“As mothers, we know that we also have a responsibility to help provide for our children and support our families’ day-to-day livelihoods. Opportunities like this will help us step up, strengthen our farming activities, and do what we can to improve the wellbeing of our households.”

While many farmers are often tempted to rely on pesticides and herbicides for convenience, access to appropriate farming tools provides practical alternatives that support organic production methods.

POLFN Farm Advisor, Amanaki Funaki, said the equipment distribution would help farmers adopt agroecological practices more effectively while reducing their dependence on chemical inputs.

" These tools are an investment in our farmers and in the future of organic agriculture in Tonga.” Amanaki said.

POLFN Project Implementation Officer, Emosi Cagi, said the distribution reflects the project's commitment to equipping farmers with the resources they need to put their training into practice.

" Through the Pacific Organic Learning Farms Network, we want to ensure they have access to the tools needed to apply agroecological practices on their farms. When farmers have both the skills and the right equipment, they are better positioned to improve their livelihoods while contributing to more sustainable and climate-resilient food systems." Cagi said.

In Vava'u, organic farmer and bishop David Lolohea believes the support will have an impact far beyond his own farm.

" As both a farmer and a church leader, I hope this support will inspire others in our community to embrace organic farming. I want to encourage more farmers to become part of this movement. By working together and sharing our experiences, we can strengthen organic farming across Vava'u and leave behind healthier land for our children.”

The equipment distribution forms part of the Pacific Organic Learning Farms Network's ongoing efforts to strengthen agroecological farming across Tonga through farmer training, peer-to-peer learning, demonstration farms, and access to appropriate farming technologies.

This work is part of the Pacific Organic Learning Farms ( POLFN ) Project under the KIWA Initiative, managed by the POETC om initiative at SPC . The KIWA initiative is funded by the European Union, Agence Françe de Développement ( AFD ), Global Affairs Canada ( GAC ), Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade ( DFAT ) and New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade ( MFAT ).

item.content:encoded:
A United States human trafficking specialist has warned that the alleged trafficking of Tongan women to China shows classic signs of human trafficking, while urging journalists and communities in Tonga to look beyond the cases already reported and investigate other forms of exploitation.

Dr Sandra Morgan, an international expert on human trafficking, made the comments during a roundtable discussion with members of the media at the U.S. Embassy in Nuku’alofa on 18 August.

Her visit followed recent reports alleging that young Tongan women had been trafficked to China through marriage arrangements. As part of her visit, Dr Morgan met with the women and described the experience as “very emotional”. Identifying human trafficking

Dr Morgan defined human trafficking as making money from another human being through the sale or exploitation of their services, including sexual services or labour.

“Human trafficking is a human rights violation. It is an economic crime because someone is making a profit from another human being,” she said.

She explained that trafficking is often understood through three elements: action, means and purpose ( AMP ). The action can include recruiting, grooming or obtaining another person through force, fraud or other forms of coercion, while the purpose is exploitation.

Asked whether she believed the situation involving the Tongan women constituted human trafficking, Dr Morgan said: “Yes. It’s a classic signs, grooming and recruiting, luring the girls with a promise of a wedding, a bride price that would help their families. Then when they get there, it’s not what they thought it would be.”

She said the circumstances appeared to involve fraud.

“Something was offered to young women, and then when they thought, ‘Well, this is better than my life here,’ and they went, and it wasn’t true. It was a lie. And so, fraud, it’s a lie. It’s offering a job that doesn’t exist, offering a life, a marriage that isn’t going to be free.”

The financial benefit to a trafficker may be direct or indirect, she said.

The International Labour Organization estimates that forced labour generates approximately US $236 billion in illegal profits every year worldwide.

Dr Morgan said many people do not understand how trafficking actually happens. Victims are sometimes blamed, making them reluctant to tell their stories because they feel ashamed, blamed and guilty, she said.

Understanding fraud, grooming and methods of luring people is therefore important to prevention. vShe said young people may have poor risk-management skills, particularly those who have already suffered abuse early in their lives.

Risks differ for each person and are often connected to individual vulnerabilities, including economic circumstances, family situations, previous abuse or a desire for a better life.

But traffickers’ goal is to make money, she said, and they look for the most vulnerable.

While much of the current attention has focused on alleged sex trafficking and marriage trafficking, Dr Morgan said labour trafficking should also be investigated.

She said she was new to working in the Pacific Islands but had already identified potential vulnerabilities associated with migrant labour.

“But I think here that a lot of the focus right now has been on sex trafficking, marriage trafficking, but I have a sense that labor trafficking has all the signs of vulnerability to that kind of crime.”

Dr Morgan draws on her work with labour-trafficking cases in California, including cases involving migrants from Asia.

For survivors, the first priority is healing from trauma, Dr Morgan said.

She compared the process to recovering from a serious car accident and spoke about the role of hope in healing, particularly for people who have spent long periods waiting for someone to come and help them.

She said rebuilding trust must happen before reintegration.

“Once they start feeling safe enough to get a vocational program, start a life where they’re entrepreneur, businesswoman, making handicrafts, so many different opportunities, but starting their own life, that’s when reintegration begins.”

Recovery should not be measured simply by whether a person has been rescued, she said.

“For most survivors, it’s at least two years before they start being okay. They’re not necessarily thriving, but they’re okay, and they can go to work.” vSurvivors need community, meaningful employment and a living wage.

“Reintegration means a real job, where you can with dignity support yourself and your child.”

“My definition of success isn’t just rescue. It’s you recover, you heal, you restore, and then you reintegrate, and that takes a few years.”

Dr Morgan encouraged communities to move beyond simply teaching children about the “red flags” of trafficking and instead teach them what healthy relationships and trusted adults look like.

“I said instead of teaching the red flags, which are often taboo, we should be teaching the green flags.”

She said children should be taught how to identify trusted adults, recognise healthy relationships and understand what healthy dating looks like.
